title: MIPLIB 2017: data-driven compilation of the 6th mixed-integer programming library
contribution: MIPLIB 2017 replaces manual committee selection with a data-driven, optimisation-based methodology (selection MIPs over 105 instance features and eight solvers' performance data) yielding a 1065-instance collection and a 240-instance benchmark set (pp. 3, 42).
problem_entry: Measured saturation of MIPLIB 2010 (virtual best/worst speed-ups 2.70 and 3.62, only 70 of 134 open instances left), posed as a fair, transparent selection problem with stated purpose and non-purpose (pp. 2-3, 20).
key_idea: Selection as a sequence of optimisation problems: diversity preselection MIPs, a collection MIP and a benchmark MIP balancing several feature and performance clusterings at once, committee rules as linear constraints (pp. 24, 28-36).
assumptions: Canonical rational MIP in MPS (Definition 1, p. 13); features on trivial presolve and row-normalised form (pp. 13-14); benchmark admission per Definition 2 (solved within 4 h, dynamism <= 10^6, no indicators, finite optimum or infeasible, p. 25); correctness only approximately enforced up to tolerance (p. 36).
proof_devices: equivalence used without proof: a feasible rational MIP has a finite optimum iff its LP relaxation has one (p. 25)
selection MIPs published but kept out of the sets (p. 42)
solution checker in GMP arbitrary precision with relative-absolute tolerance test (pp. 22-23)
exact objective values via SoPlex iterative refinement after fixing integers (p. 42)
max-min diversity preselection MIP with product linearisation (pp. 26-27)
experiments: Eight solvers, 4 h limit, almost 40 CPU years on 5721 instances, reported only as virtual best/median/worst (pp. 20-22); instrument evaluation: epsilon sensitivity (Table 10, p. 33), feature-space validation against model groups (p. 37), hardness vs MIPLIB 2010 (pp. 39-40), one-sided KS tests per solver (pp. 40-41); no per-solver results, no variability or seeds (pp. 36, 38).
positioning: Lineage of reporting standards (Hoffman et al. 1953, Crowder-Dembo-Mulvey, Jackson et al.), presented as an extension of Hooker's idea of problem choice as experimental design; earlier MIPLIBs not criticised; own group's tools supply the pipeline (pp. 1-6, 12-23, 44).
writing: Contribution stated twice (pp. 3, 42); hand-made choices conceded up front and at the close (pp. 3-4, 43); named instances carry the argument; admissions in footnotes; limits paragraph inside the method section (p. 36); committee voice throughout (p. 44).
limits_future: Difficulty representation 'not even well-defined': snapshot, time limit, no variability or parallel scaling, tolerance-only correctness (p. 36); not a general blueprint (p. 43); post-release minimal update for two flawed instances (pp. 43-44, fn. 8); future hindsight study and preselection comparison (p. 43).

transferable: Max-min diversity selection of κ items from a group: maximise z with z ≤ (d_ij − d̄) x_i x_j + d̄, Σ x_i = κ, a must-cover side constraint, and the product linearised by w_ij ≤ x_i, w_ij ≤ x_j, w_ij ≥ x_i + x_j − 1 (pp. 26–27).

Balance against several clusterings at once: (1 − ε) δ y_k ≤ Σ_{i∈C} x_i ≤ (1 + ε) δ y_k per cluster, the lower side dropped for small clusters and the upper side for boxplot-outlier clusters, δ the shifted geometric mean of within-cluster distances (pp. 29–31).

Per-solver performance clusterings (absolute rank, relative time with a shift, exponential time bins; timeouts split by how many other solvers finished), so that no solver looks different on the subset than on the pool (pp. 33–35).
A hardness tilt in the selection objective, 1 + (1/20) √(virtual-best time), with a knapsack budget on capped median times, checked afterwards for whether the budget binds (pp. 35–36).

Solution-checker violation test in arbitrary precision: a_i x* − u_i ≤ ε · max{(a_i x*)^+, (a_i x*)^−, |u_i|, 1} with ε = 10^-5; bounds and objective checked the same way, integrality with an absolute 10^-4 (p. 23).

Inconsistency rule for benchmark admission: a verified primal value below another solver's dual bound or infeasibility claim makes the instance ambiguous; exclude it unless an obvious bug in one solver explains the conflict (p. 23).
Compute instance features after a trivial presolve iterated to a fixed point, with rows normalised by their largest coefficient and log or siglog scaling, and ship the extractor (pp. 13–16).
Validate a feature space by P(similar pair | same group) against P(similar pair), then repeat without the groups derived from the features (p. 37).
One-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov test per solver for whether the subset is harder than the pool, printing the solvers where it is not significant (pp. 40–41).
A sensitivity table for the key free constant, including the settings where the model becomes infeasible (Table 10, p. 33).
Versioned download files, and exact objective values of reported solutions by fixing the integers and solving the remaining LP exactly with iterative refinement (p. 42).
Memorable suffixes for anonymous numeric instance names (neos-xyz-river, skipping ambiguous rivers such as Amazon, p. 10).

quotes.text: Despite the heavy use of quantitative methodology, the overall process inherently requires many manual decisions and heuristic choices.
Instances exhibiting such ambiguity are not suitable for benchmarking, since handling this numerical ambiguity can be done in different ways, requiring different amounts of computational effort.
